title: The story that healed
hookLine: a lame grandfather told how the Baal Shem danced while praying, and began to dance himself

lines: FOR A MOMENT, HE'S IN THE ROOM.
cards: At a family dinner, someone starts telling a story about a grandparent who's gone, and halfway through, they start doing the voice. The walk. The laugh.
For a moment, the person is almost in the room. A good story doesn't just describe something. It brings it back.
Hasidim took that seriously. Today, the story they tell about why they tell stories at all.

teach.b: A rabbi, whose grandfather had been a student of the Baal Shem Tov, was once asked to tell a story. He said: a story ought to be told so that it helps. And he told this one.
My grandfather was lame. One day people asked him to tell a story about his teacher, the Baal Shem Tov.

teach.h: THE BAAL SHEM DANCED AS HE PRAYED.
teach.b: So he told them how the holy Baal Shem used to leap and dance while he prayed. And as he told it, my grandfather stood up.
He got so carried away by the story that he began to leap and dance, to show how his master had done it. And from that hour on, he was healed. That, said the rabbi, is how to tell a story.
One small story holds the whole movement inside it. Hasidim didn't treat their tales as entertainment.
They told them at the Shabbat table, at the end of a festival, on the anniversary of a teacher's death, believing that telling of a holy deed could stir up the same holiness in the people listening.

Look back at this stretch: the Baal Shem Tov and serving with joy, the shepherd boy's whistle, the alphabet prayer, the fire and the place, Zusya, two pockets, the defense attorney, the tailor, the narrow bridge, the lost princess, the turkey prince, the crying baby, the tavern, the rebbe with the axe, the niggun, the sparks, the Maggid's circle, the Mitnagdim.
Tomorrow, a new stretch: the Psalms, the songs of Jewish prayer.

how: Hasidim tell stories of their rebbes at the Shabbat table, at gatherings, and especially on a teacher's yahrzeit, the anniversary of his death, as a way of drawing close to his holiness.

practice: Pick one story that lifts you, from these Hasidic tales, maybe the shepherd boy's whistle, or from your own life, maybe something your grandmother did.
Tell it to yourself quietly, in your own words, the way you'd tell it to a friend, and notice where it lifts. If you pray, give thanks for the people in your stories.
